headline: Ship queue grows to 48 as berthing stays slow
brief: Last night 48 container ships were waiting, up from 33 a week earlier, while only about 3.0 ships a day reached a berth. Dividing the queue by that berthing rate suggests a ship joining today could wait about 16 days. The published 7-day average of 7.1 days looks backward at ships already berthed, so it likely understates the wait for new arrivals.
watch: Watch whether daily berthings rise above 3.0 ships, since the queue keeps growing if they do not.

facts.how_the_published_figure_works: average wait of ships that reached a berth in the last 7 days, so it looks backward

watch: Watch whether daily berthings stay near 4.3 ships, since a slower pace would push waits past the 14-day estimate.

headline: Offshore waiting rule hides part of the ship queue
brief: The published 7-day average wait is 14.9 days, but it only looks backward at ships that already reached a berth, about 4.0 per day. Since today, container ships wait about 150 nm offshore, beyond shore AIS range, so we cannot count that queue or estimate its wait. Yesterday's counts, 43.6 at anchor and 57.8 loitering within 60 nm, may now understate the true backlog.
watch: Watch whether the anchorage count drops simply because ships moved out of range, not because the backlog is easing.

facts.how_the_published_figure_works: average wait of ships that reached a berth in the last 7 days, so it looks backward
facts.rule_change: Since Nov 16 2021, container ships are told to wait about 150 nm offshore instead of at the anchorage. That is beyond shore AIS range, so we cannot count that queue or estimate its wait.
